title: Emergencies & Crashes
summary: How to handle brake, tire and engine failures, skids, stalls on tracks or in water, and what the law expects of you after a crash.

blocks.text: If your brakes fail, stay calm and work through these steps in order. Keep steering the whole time. (Pumping is only for failed brakes; in a normal hard stop with ABS, see the table below.)

items: If the pedal sinks to the floor, take your foot off the gas and pump the brake pedal fast and hard several times. This can build up enough pressure to stop.
If pumping does not help, apply the parking (emergency) brake slowly. Hold the release so you can ease off if the rear wheels lock and the car starts to skid.
Shift to a lower gear if you can, and look for a safe place to stop off the road.
Once stopped, call for help. Do not drive on until the brakes are repaired.

blocks.text: Never turn the key to Lock while the car is moving; the steering wheel can lock. If the engine is shut off, power steering and power brakes lose their assist, so expect to steer and brake much harder.

If the brake warning light comes on and the pedal sinks farther than normal before the car slows, part of the brake system may have failed. Many cars can still brake on two wheels, so slow down, pull off safely and have the brakes checked.

rows: Press the pedal hard and hold steady pressure. Do not pump. Pulsing, grinding or buzzing means ABS is working, so keep pressing and steer around the hazard.
Brake firmly, just short of locking the wheels. If they lock, ease off so the wheels roll again, then reapply more gently.
A sliding car with locked wheels will not steer. Release enough brake to let the wheels turn, and steering comes back.

blocks.text: The big advantage of ABS is that you can keep steering while braking hard. It does not always stop you shorter and does not replace a safe following distance.

sections.heading: Blowouts and running off the pavement

blocks.text: A steady thumping from a wheel can warn of a tire about to fail or a loose wheel. Pull safely off the road and check your tires.

items: Blowout: grip the steering wheel firmly with both hands and keep the car going straight.
Ease off the gas slowly and let the car slow down. Do not brake hard or steer sharply.
When the car is stable and slower, brake gently and pull completely off the road.
If there is no shoulder, drive slowly on the flat to a safe spot ahead. A ruined rim is better than stopping in a travel lane.

blocks.text: If your right wheels drop off the pavement onto a soft shoulder:

items: Stay calm, hold the wheel firmly and take your foot off the gas. Do not brake hard.
Straddle the pavement edge and let the car slow down.
When your speed is low and traffic is clear, steer gently back onto the road.

blocks.text: Jerking the wheel to climb the pavement edge at speed can make the car shoot across the road into oncoming traffic.

items: Ease your foot off the gas. Avoid hard braking, which can lock the wheels and make the skid worse.
Look and steer where you want the car to go. Drivers tend to steer toward whatever they stare at.
If the rear of the car slides, steer in the same direction the rear is sliding. Rear sliding right means steer right. Do not oversteer.
If the rear then slides the other way, steer smoothly that way too. Keep correcting as many times as needed until the car is straight.

blocks.text: Without ABS, locked wheels are often the cause of a skid. Let off the brake so the wheels roll and steering returns.

rows: Shift to neutral, brake, and steer to a safe place off the road. The engine may roar in neutral; that is normal. Turn the engine off once stopped.
Power steering and power brakes lose their assist but still work. Grip firmly, brake harder than usual and pull off the road.
Ease off the gas, turn on your flashers, and once the car slows, brake very gently to a stop. A sudden speed change can throw you out of control.
Work the headlight and dimmer (high/low) switches first. If that fails, use flashers, parking lights or turn signals and pull off the road.
Look through the gap under the hood or out your side window while you slow down and pull off.

items: Pull as far off the road as you can and turn on your emergency flashers.
Do not stop just over the top of a hill or just around a curve, where others cannot see you in time.
Place warning triangles or flares behind your car, facing approaching traffic.
If you must get out, exit on the side away from traffic and stay clear of the lanes. Do not stand behind the car, where you hide the taillights and stand in the path of a crash.

blocks.caption: Many states require drivers to move over or slow down for stopped vehicles with flashing lights. Details vary; see your State Cheat Sheet.

items: Smoke from under the hood: pull off the road and turn off the ignition. Most vehicle fires start in the electrical system.
Your top priority is people. Get everyone out and well away from the car, then call 911.
Never use water on a gasoline fire. Burning gas floats on water and the fire spreads. Use an extinguisher, sand or dirt, and get far away if it is not quickly controlled.
Steam usually means overheating. Leave the radiator cap closed until the engine cools; opening it hot can spray boiling coolant.

blocks.text: Carbon monoxide (CO) in exhaust is a deadly gas you cannot see or smell. Warning signs include headache, dizziness, nausea, tiredness and yawning.
If you suspect CO poisoning, get the person into fresh air right away and call 911. Then have the exhaust system checked.

sections.heading: Stalled on railroad tracks or in water

items: If a train is coming, get everyone out right away. A train cannot stop quickly, and your car is not worth your life.
Move away from the tracks at an angle toward the oncoming train. Wreckage is thrown forward in the direction the train is moving.
If the crossing lights are flashing but you cannot see a train, get out anyway. A train may be seconds away.
If no train is in sight, call the railroad using the number on the blue Emergency Notification System sign at the crossing. If you cannot find it, call 911.

blocks.text: If your car goes into deep water:

items: While the car is still floating, unbuckle and escape through a window. Opening a door lets water rush in.
Open power windows immediately, before water shorts out the electrical system. If they will not open, try to break a side window.
If the car sinks first, find the air pocket near the roof at the back. Most cars sink nose first. Take a breath, then get out through a window.
Call 911 only after you are out of the car.

blocks.text: You have three ways to avoid a collision: stop, steer away, or speed up. At highway speed, steering into a clear lane is often quicker than stopping.

items: Car coming at you in your lane: slow down, move right (even onto the shoulder) and sound your horn. Do not swerve left; the other driver may swerve back into that lane.
About to be hit from the side or from behind, with clear space ahead: speeding up can get you out of the way. Slow down again once you are clear.
About to be hit from behind with nowhere to go: press your head against the head restraint, brace, and be ready to brake so you are not pushed into others.
About to be hit from the side: keep a firm grip on the wheel and be ready to steer if the car spins.

rows: Something that gives way, like bushes or shrubs
A vehicle moving the same direction as you

blocks.text: If you must hit something, steer even slightly to make it a glancing blow instead of a head-on hit.

items: Stop. Every driver involved must stop, no matter how small the damage. Leaving is a hit-and-run.
If anyone is hurt, call 911 right away. Police must always be told about crashes with injury or death.
If no one is hurt and the cars can be driven, move them out of traffic. Do not leave the scene.
Exchange names, addresses, license numbers, plate and vehicle details, and insurance company and policy numbers. Note any witnesses.
Report the crash as your state requires. Reporting rules for property damage vary; see your State Cheat Sheet.
Do not move an injured person unless they are in immediate danger, such as from fire. If you must, keep the back and neck as straight as possible.
For heavy bleeding, press firmly on the wound with a cloth or your hand.
If a power line falls on the car, stay inside and warn others to stay away until help arrives.
If you hit an unattended car and cannot find the owner, securely leave a note with your name and contact information, and notify police.

keyPoints: Brake failure: pump the pedal, then apply the parking brake slowly and shift to a lower gear. In a hard stop with ABS, press hard and hold; do not pump.
Blowout: grip the wheel, keep straight, ease off the gas, and brake gently only after the car is under control.
In a skid, ease off the gas and steer where you want to go, in the direction the rear is sliding.
Stuck gas pedal: shift to neutral, brake and steer off the road.
Stalled on tracks with a train coming: get out and move away at an angle toward the train.
In water, escape through a window right away; call 911 once you are out.
To avoid a crash, steer, stop or speed up. If you must hit something, pick something soft or moving your way, and aim for a glancing blow.
After any crash, stop, help the injured, call 911 if anyone is hurt, and exchange information.
